title: Asymptotically optimal algorithms for random three-dimensional assignment
formal: Is there a uniform polynomial-time algorithm \(A\) and a deterministic sequence \(\eta_n\ge0\) with \(\eta_n\to0\) such that, for an \(n\times n\times n\) array of independent mean-one exponential costs, \(A\) returns permutations \(\pi,\sigma\in S_n\) satisfying \[\Pr\!\left[\sum_{i=1}^n C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\le(1+\eta_n)\operatorname{OPT}(C)\right]\longrightarrow1?\] The dimension is exactly three and the assignment is axial, as defined below.
definitions:
Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\) and \(S_n\) for its permutations. The \(n^3\) input coordinates \(C_{ijk}\) are mutually independent with \(\Pr[C_{ijk}>t]=e^{-t}\) for \(t\ge0\). A feasible assignment is the set of \(n\) triples \((i,\pi(i),\sigma(i))\); each label in each coordinate position occurs once. Define \(\operatorname{OPT}(C)=\min_{\pi,\sigma\in S_n}\sum_i C_{i,\pi(i),\sigma(i)}\). It is positive with probability one. The question concerns approximation to the realized optimum of the same array, not to its expectation.

The array is explicitly accessible in random-access memory, with each real entry read at unit cost. Use exact real arithmetic with addition, subtraction, multiplication, nonzero division and comparison, ordinary indexing and fair random bits, each at unit cost. No unit-cost operation exposes infinitely many bits of an input real. A finite program must run in at most \(Cn^c\) operations on every nonnegative input and every random tape, for some absolute constants \(C,c\). Polynomial time in \(n\) is also polynomial in the array length \(n^3\). The algorithm always returns two permutations; its approximation guarantee is only probabilistic. This explicitly chosen arithmetic model does not claim a bit-complexity result for finitely rounded costs.

Probability is jointly over the independent input array and any internal coins, taken independently. No success guarantee is required for each individual array. The same algorithm works for all \(n\); \(\eta_n\) is independent of the realized costs and no particular convergence rate is prescribed. Thus a scheme giving a separate algorithm for every fixed accuracy does not by itself state the required single polynomial-time, vanishing-relative-error guarantee.

The planar three-dimensional assignment problem imposes one chosen entry on each axis-parallel line and selects \(n^2\) entries. That is a different feasible set. This card instead imposes one entry in each coordinate plane and selects \(n\) entries.
answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked affirmative proof supplying the algorithm, polynomial bound, vanishing error sequence and probability limit, or a complete Lean-checked proof that no such algorithm exists in the stated model. Bounding the optimum's expected value, giving a constant approximation factor, or obtaining an \(n^{o(1)}\) factor does not suffice for a factor tending to one. A runtime or quality guarantee confined to the planar variant does not answer this axial question.
context:
Frieze and Sorkin distinguish axial and planar assignments and ask about polynomial-time optimal or near-optimal algorithms for independent exponential costs. Their axial result obtains cost of order at most n to the power −1 plus a vanishing term, while the elementary lower scale is inverse-linear. This does not establish relative error tending to zero.

The benchmark selects the asymptotically optimal approximation question from the supplied catalogue. It does not ask for the limiting optimum-cost constant or require exact optimization. The runtime and probability quantifiers above make the catalogue interpretation explicit.

import_provenance.original_statement: For independent Exp(1) costs C_{i,j,k}, find permutations π,σ minimizing Σ_i C_{i,π(i),σ(i)}. Is there a polynomial-time algorithm whose cost is (1+o(1)) times optimum with high probability, extending the strong algorithmic understanding of two-dimensional random assignment?

sentences: An instance contains independent exponential costs for all triples of three equal-sized label sets.
A feasible axial assignment uses every label exactly once.
The question asks for one polynomial-time algorithm whose relative error vanishes with high probability.
The cited efficient bound has a subpolynomial approximation factor and does not establish this guarantee.
A resolution would clarify whether random higher-dimensional assignment admits algorithmic asymptotic optimality.
